We want to understand what you meant by "the "Continue Shopping" part feels very prominent, almost maybe too much?", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The large size and bold styling of the "Continue Shopping" button compared to the "Place Order" button.
B) The high placement of the "Continue Shopping" option within the primary action area at the bottom of the screen.
C) The visual weight of the "Continue Shopping" label relative to the other elements in the final checkout section.
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: I—well, I think it's mostly... well, it's probably option A. The way "Continue Shopping" is in that dark box makes it look so much more active than the "Place Order" button, which looks almost grayed out or... I mean, it just feels like my eyes go straight to that one first because of the contrast. It might be a bit confusing for someone trying to actually finish their purchase, but again, I'm not sure if that's what the designers intended.

turns.q: What specific information were you looking for when your eyes landed on the "Continue Shopping" button?
turns.a: I—well, it’s hard to say exactly what I was looking for... I think my eye just jumped there because of the high contrast. Because the "Continue Shopping" button is such a heavy, dark block, it feels like... well, it's much more visually prominent than the other elements around it. It almost seems like it's pulling focus away from the actual checkout process, but I could be wrong about why that's happening.

turns.q: What specific part of this wireframe's visual hierarchy were you evaluating when the size difference between those two buttons stood out?
turns.a: I—well, I think it was really just the... well, the very bottom section where both buttons are grouped together. Because "Continue Shopping" is in that large, dark block and "Place Order" is so much lighter, it feels like they're competing for attention. It’s hard to say if that was intentional, but because of the way they're stacked right next to each other, the contrast makes the primary goal—the order—feel almost secondary, I guess... but that might just be my own interpretation.

turns.q: When you first looked at this wireframe, what was your primary focus or goal as you scanned the layout?
turns.a: I—well, I think my initial instinct was to... well, it was probably just trying to find where to complete the transaction. Because "Place Order" is usually the final step in a checkout process, that's what I expected to be the main focus. But because of the way the buttons are styled, I found myself looking at the "Continue Shopping" box first, which... well, it made me pause for a second to see if I was even on the right page.

turns.q: As you were scanning this specific screen, what was your initial goal or focus area before the button styling caught your eye?
turns.a: I—well, I think my main focus... well, it was probably just trying to identify the "success" path. Because when you're looking at a checkout page like this one, you're really just looking for the way to finish the transaction. I mean, even before I noticed the buttons were different, I was scanning for the final confirmation step, which... well, it should have been the most obvious thing on the screen, but the layout made me hesitate slightly.

turns.q: When you first looked at this screen, what specific part of the layout were you evaluating that made the button contrast stand out to you?
turns.a: I—well, I think it was really just the... well, the very bottom section where both buttons are grouped together. Because "Continue Shopping" is in that large, dark block and "Place Order" is so much lighter, it feels like they're competing for attention. It’s hard to say if that was intentional, but because of the way they're stacked right next to each other, the contrast makes the primary goal—the order—feel almost secondary, I guess... but that might just be my own interpretation.

turns.q: What would need to be true about the visual relationship between these two buttons for you to feel confident that the checkout process is the clear primary path?
turns.a: I—well, I think it might... well, if the "Place Order" button had more visual weight than the "Continue Shopping" one. Specifically, I think making "Place Order" a darker or bolder color would make it feel like the intended next step. Right now, because "Continue Shopping" is such a heavy block and "Place Order" is so light, it feels almost like... well, like the system is encouraging me to stay on the site rather than finishing the purchase, which I'm not sure is what they want.
